market_scope: supermarket consumer goods / POS regular and sale prices
note: Many items passed through the 2014 increase, but pass-through differed across goods and both under- and over-shifting occurred. No uniform household pass-through coefficient is promoted.

market_scope: taxable CPI items excluding reduced-rate items
note: BOJ assumed full pass-through for taxable items when mechanically estimating the direct CPI effect; this is an assumption, not an empirical pass-through estimate.

policy_change: VAT standard rate 8% to 10% with reduced rate
note: BOJ separated front-loaded demand/subsequent decline from the real-income channel. This does not identify a steady-state quantity elasticity for a VAT cut or abolition.

source_locator: 2014 Japanese Economy, ch.1 sec.1, Table 1-1-4 discussion
note: Cabinet Office estimated 2014 front-loading and rebound at 2.5-3.3 trillion yen, about 0.5-0.6% of real GDP; this is timing substitution around a tax increase, not a persistent demand multiplier.

policy_change: temporary broad VAT rate cut, then restoration
method: web-scraped daily prices; Germany-vs-Austria causal comparison
note: Temporary German VAT cut lowered supermarket prices by roughly 1.3%, implying about 70% cut pass-through. The subsequent VAT increase price effect was only about half as large, so simple cut/increase symmetry is not supported in this study scope.

policy_change: temporary standard VAT cut by 2.5 percentage points
note: Firms initially lowered prices, but part of pass-through reversed within months. Retail sales volume rose around 1% (about 0.4% total-expenditure effect by itself) and fell significantly after the cut ended, indicating intertemporal substitution.
Reduced 8% applies to specified food/beverages excluding liquor and dining out, and qualifying subscribed newspapers; category rules do not identify decile-specific taxable expenditure shares.
